syllabus.clause: unified memory manager: execution vs storage regions with borrowing and eviction (spark.memory.fraction, storageFraction), user memory, reserved memory, off-heap, and memoryOverhead for netty buffers, Python workers and native libraries; JVM OutOfMemoryError vs container OOM-kill (YARN/Kubernetes) and why they need different fixes.

at.step: Reveal: no — fully evicted, and still spills
Reveal: one leaves a trace, one leaves nothing
Elaborate: why they need different fixes

at.deep: User memory, reserved memory, and off-heap

sources.source: UnifiedMemoryManager.scala (Apache Spark source, GitHub, tag v4.0.0)

items.item: a soft boundary lets either side borrow from the other; storage's borrowed memory gets evicted when execution reclaims it, but execution's borrowed memory is never evicted by storage
the unified pool's size is (heap - 300MB reserved) * memory.fraction, with storageFraction further splitting it into execution and storage regions

memoryOverhead covers VM overhead, interned strings, off-heap memory, and other co-located processes (a PySpark driver's own Python process) that the JVM heap never tracks; a container's real ceiling is memory + memoryOverhead together

at.step: Elaborate: why they need different fixes

items.item: User memory (everything above the unified pool but below the reserved 300MB) holds user-defined data structures, Spark-internal metadata, and large records that don't go through either the execution or storage pool -- it's not a third borrowable region, it's simply unmanaged heap outside the unified manager's accounting entirely.

at.out: user memory's own definition named only; this topic's own examples.py measures inside the unified pool, not the user-memory region above it

items.item: The 300MB reserved-memory carve-out exists specifically so small heaps don't starve: a 1GB JVM still gets a usable (1024-300)*0.6=434MB pool rather than a vanishingly small one, per the source's own worked example -- this topic's own measured pool size for a 768MB heap follows the identical formula.

at.out: the reserved-memory rationale named only beyond the formula itself; this topic's own examples.py verifies the formula's output, not why 300MB specifically was chosen

items.item: spark.memory.offHeap.enabled moves the entire unified pool off the JVM heap into native (direct) memory, sized by spark.memory.offHeap.size instead of being derived from spark.executor.memory at all -- a configuration this topic's own examples.py never enables, measuring only the default on-heap pool.

at.out: off-heap memory's own separate sizing mechanism named only; this topic's own examples.py measures only the on-heap unified pool

items.item: memoryOverhead's own default (max(384MB, executorMemory * 0.1)) means a large executor gets a proportionally large overhead allowance automatically, while a small executor can still be starved by a fixed 384MB floor if its actual off-heap/native footprint exceeds that floor -- this topic's own measured container-kill case (disclosed in FACT-CHECK.md) used a cgroup limit set independently of this formula, not derived from it.

at.out: the memoryOverhead default formula's own two-regime behavior named only; this topic's own measured container-kill case sets the cgroup limit directly rather than deriving it from this formula

items.item: Python workers in PySpark run as entirely separate OS processes from the JVM executor, communicating over a socket -- their own memory footprint is counted toward memoryOverhead (or a dedicated spark.executor.pyspark.memory budget), never toward the JVM heap the unified manager governs, which is why a Python UDF that leaks memory produces a container-level symptom, not a JVM heap OOM.

at.out: the Python-worker-memory distinction named only; this topic's own measured heap-OOM case uses a pure Scala/JVM-side collect, not a Python UDF

items.item: Netty's own off-heap buffer pool (used for shuffle and RPC network transfers) is accounted toward memoryOverhead specifically because Netty allocates outside the JVM heap by design, for zero-copy transfers -- a third source of non-heap growth alongside off-heap storage memory and Python workers, named directly in the memoryOverhead syllabus clause.

at.out: Netty's own off-heap allocation reason named only; this topic's own measured scenarios don't isolate network-buffer growth specifically

items.item: On YARN and Kubernetes specifically, exceeding the memory+memoryOverhead ceiling produces a container-manager-level kill (YARN's NodeManager, or the kubelet via cgroups) rather than any Spark-internal code path -- Spark itself has no opportunity to log or react, which is exactly why this topic's own measured cgroup-kill case shows zero Spark-side exception text anywhere.

at.out: which specific component (NodeManager vs kubelet) performs the kill on each platform, named only; this topic's own measured case uses a raw Linux cgroup directly, not a real YARN or Kubernetes cluster

items.item: A fix for a JVM heap OOM (raise spark.executor.memory, lower per-task memory demand, or raise memory.fraction) can make a container OOM-kill worse rather than better if memoryOverhead isn't raised in step with it, since the container's own ceiling is the sum of both -- the two failure modes don't just need different fixes, the naive fix for one can actively cause the other.

at.out: the fix-for-one-worsens-the-other interaction named only, as a practical consequence beyond the recap's own two-separate-fixes framing; this topic's own examples.py measures each failure mode's symptom, not the effect of a specific remediation

items.item: Spilling (the next topic) is execution memory's own last-resort fallback once it can no longer borrow enough from storage -- this topic's own measured eviction case shows the two happening together (full eviction, then spill anyway), establishing that eviction alone is not always sufficient to satisfy an execution memory request.

at.out: the composition with spill as the next escalation step, named only; the full mechanics of spill itself are this chapter's next topic, not re-taught here

items.item: A cached dataset using Serialized vs Deserialized storage levels changes how much of the storage region a given row count actually occupies -- MEMORY_ONLY (deserialized by default for RDDs, but Datasets/DataFrames cache serialized by default) can use significantly less space than a naive per-row estimate would suggest, which is why this topic's own examples.py measures actual bytes reported by Spark's own storage API rather than estimating from row counts.

at.out: the serialized-vs-deserialized storage-level sizing distinction named only; this topic's own examples.py reads the real reported byte counts directly rather than relying on an estimate
